# 1.1 - Frequency Tables, Dot Plots, and Histograms {.unnumbered}

Eleven students say how many siblings they have:

:::{.text-center}
1, 0, 2, 1, 1, 3, 2, 0, 1, 2, 4
:::

What number is most common? It is hard to see in a list. A table or a graph makes it easy to see.

In this lesson, you learn three ways to show {{< glink data >}}: frequency tables, dot plots, and histograms.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I make and read a frequency table.
- [ ] I make and read a dot plot.
- [ ] I make and read a histogram.
:::

:::{.vocab}
{{< glink data >}},
{{< glink frequency >}},
{{< glink "frequency table" >}},
{{< glink tally >}},
{{< glink "dot plot" >}},
{{< glink histogram >}},
{{< glink bin >}}
:::

{{< learn >}}

### 1.1.1 - Frequency Tables

{{< glink frequency text="Frequency" >}} means **how many times** something happens.

A {{< glink "frequency table" >}} lists each value and its frequency. Read the data one value at a time. Make a {{< glink tally >}} mark for each one. Then count the marks.

Here is the siblings data:

| Siblings | Tally | Frequency |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | \|\| | 2 |
| 1 | \|\|\|\| | 4 |
| 2 | \|\|\| | 3 |
| 3 | \| | 1 |
| 4 | \| | 1 |

The most common number of siblings is **1**.

:::{.remember title="Check Your Count"}
Add the frequency column. The total should equal the number of data values.

$$2 + 4 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 11 \text{ students}$$
:::

***

### 1.1.2 - Dot Plots

A {{< glink "dot plot" >}} puts the values on a number line. Each value gets **one dot**. Dots for the same value stack up.

This dot plot shows the same siblings data:

![](/images/Unit_1/1.1_dot_plot_siblings.svg){width="320px" fig-align="center"}

The height of each stack is the frequency. The stack above 1 is the tallest, so 1 is the most common.

:::{.you-try-m title="Read the dot plot above."}
a. How many students have 2 siblings?

b. How many students have more than 1 sibling?
:::
:::{.answer title="Answer"}
a. The stack above 2 has **3** dots.

b. Count the dots above 2, 3, and 4: $3 + 1 + 1 = 5$ students.
:::

***

### 1.1.3 - Histograms

A {{< glink histogram >}} is a bar graph for number data. The values are put into groups called {{< glink slug="bin" text="bins" >}}. Each bar is one bin.

![](/images/Unit_1/1.1_histogram_heights.svg){width="380px" fig-align="center"}

The tallest bar is 170 to 180. So 7 students are from 170 cm to 180 cm tall.

There are **no gaps** between the bars. The bins touch, like the numbers on a number line.

:::{.remember title="The Histogram Rule"}
If a value is **on a line** between two bars, it goes in the bar on the **right**.

160 goes in the 160 to 170 bar.
:::

:::{.gotcha title="A histogram hides the exact values"}
The graph shows that 6 students are from 160 cm to 170 cm. It does **not** show their exact heights. A dot plot shows every value. A histogram does not.
:::

:::{.think title="When is a histogram better than a dot plot?"}
When there is a lot of data, or the values are spread out.

Heights in centimeters can be 158, 163, 171, 179, and so on. A dot plot would have many short stacks. A histogram groups them, so the shape is easy to see.
:::

:::{.remember title="Every Time You Read a Graph"}
1. Read the title.
2. Read both axis labels.
3. Check the scale.
:::

{{< practice >}}

Work with a partner. Compare answers when you finish each problem.

**Dot Plots**

1. This dot plot shows how many pets some students have.

   ![](/images/Unit_1/1.1_dot_plot_pets.svg){width="360px"}

   a. How many students have exactly 2 pets?

   b. How many students are in the data?

   c. How many students have more than 2 pets?

   d. What number of pets is most common?

2. A soccer team scored these goals in 12 games. Make a dot plot.

   2, 0, 1, 3, 1, 1, 4, 2, 0, 1, 2, 1

***

**Frequency Tables**

3. 20 students said how many siblings they have. Make a frequency table.

   1, 2, 0, 3, 1, 1, 2, 4, 0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 5, 2, 1

   a. How many students have 2 or more siblings?

   b. How can you use your table to check that you counted everyone?

4. This frequency table shows how many hours some students slept last night.

   | Hours of sleep | Frequency |
   |:---:|:---:|
   | 5 | 2 |
   | 6 | 4 |
   | 7 | 6 |
   | 8 | 5 |
   | 9 | 3 |

   a. How many students are in the data?

   b. How many students slept less than 7 hours?

   c. Make a dot plot of the same data.

***

**Histograms**

5. This histogram shows how many minutes some students take to get to school.

   ![](/images/Unit_1/1.1_histogram_minutes.svg){width="440px"}

   a. How many students take from 20 to 30 minutes?

   b. How many students take less than 20 minutes?

   c. How many students are in the data?

   d. Can you tell from this graph how many students take exactly 15 minutes? Explain.

6. A basketball player scored these points in 15 games.

   12, 8, 15, 21, 9, 14, 18, 10, 25, 13, 7, 16, 20, 11, 19

   a. Make a frequency table with the bins 5 to 10, 10 to 15, 15 to 20, 20 to 25, and 25 to 30. Remember the histogram rule.

   b. Make a histogram. Label both axes.
